venues.d: The city's grande dame since 1844 — family-owned, lake-facing, and quietly the address that matters.
A fairy-tale hillside resort above Zurich — a spa, an art collection and the whole lake laid out below.
The city's oldest grand hotel, reborn — Mandarin Oriental precision on the Paradeplatz.
Nine medieval townhouses stitched into one — an art-and-design masterpiece in the heart of the Old Town.

venues.n: La Réserve Eden au Lac Zurich
venues.d: A Philippe Starck-imagined 'yacht club' on the lake — playful, private and thoroughly of the moment.
Six hundred years on the Limmat — a riverfront address woven into the fabric of the Old Town.
Cool, contemporary calm a step from Bahnhofstrasse — glass, art and space where the city is dense.
A restored 15th-century house in the pedestrian Old Town — design-led, intimate, and full of history.
An all-suite mansion of 1895 — quiet, discreet, and among the most private addresses in the city.
A Marcel Wanders design spectacle on the city's edge — bold, playful, and unlike anything in the Old Town.
A witty, design-forward base in the reinvented industrial west — excellent value by Zurich standards.
Heiko Nieder's classical-modern cooking, laced with exotic accents — the city's benchmark table, high above the lake.
Stefan Heilemann bridges classic haute cuisine and Thai-inflected modernity — the Old Town's two-star jewel.
Mitja Birlo's surprise menu at a U-shaped counter beside the open kitchen — two stars from a standing start, inside the station.
Caminada's fine-dining-meets-sharing concept — generous, playful and technically exact.
Dario Moresco's creative modern Italian, guided by Milan's two-star Antonio Guida — bold contrasts, beautifully balanced.
Refined cooking in a 14th-century riverside room — the Limmat gliding past the window.
Sebastian Rösch's precise, light cooking — classical foundations with a bright, modern hand.
Entirely vegan fine dining with Moroccan and Mexican accents — creative, seasonal and quietly radical.
Nenad Mlinarevic's purely vegetarian, market-driven cooking in the heart of the Old Town.
An intimate Japanese counter — omakase sushi for a handful of guests, prepared before you.
Modern Italian with a namesake cellar — Bolgheri's great wines beside a considered kitchen.
Markus Stöckle's self-styled 'neo-Bavarian' room — vivid, warm and unexpectedly refined.
Julian Marti's small, values-led kitchen — food, wine and service in quiet, sustainable harmony.
Nikkei cooking — Peru meets Japan — on a lively rooftop above the shopping street.
A Zurich institution since 1924 — Swiss and Viennese classics served beneath Chagall, Picasso and Miró.
The Baur au Lac's signature room — Mediterranean-leaning cooking with the hotel's long-held polish.
A deluxe brasserie of the classics — Zürcher Geschnetzeltes and sole done immaculately.
Masami Okamoto's exclusive omakase for a few guests a night — pure, exacting Japanese craft.
A modern izakaya of real quality — Japanese small plates and charcoal, at an honest price.
Contemporary Turkish over wood and charcoal — a bright surprise menu that punches far above its price.
Antonio Colaianni's lively trattoria — vitello tonnato and tiramisù finished at your table.
Honest Swiss cooking — sausage, rösti and beer done properly, without a shred of ceremony.

A leafy hilltop terrace on the site of a Roman fort and later imperial palace, shaded by century-old linden trees, with one of the loveliest free views over the Limmat, the Old Town spires and Grossmünster. Locals play boules and chess here; a calm, camera-ready pause on a private walking tour, and a favourite spot for a golden-hour photograph.

The pedestrianised heart of the Old Town — cobbled alleys winding up toward the Grossmünster, lined with boutiques, chocolatiers, cafés and long-standing patisseries. Best explored slowly on foot, ideally early evening; a private guide can thread you past the Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse and the quieter courtyards the crowds miss.

One of the most expensive shopping streets in the world, running from the main station to the lake. This is where Zurich's watches and jewellery live — the maisons, the grandes marques, and the great multi-brand houses — alongside international fashion. Stroll it end to end, then reward the family at Sprüngli on Paradeplatz. A concierge can arrange private after-hours appointments at the watch houses.

One of the world's oldest watch and jewellery houses, family-run since 1760, and a serious address for Patek Philippe, Rolex and the finest independents. The ground-floor salon is discreet and unhurried; ask for a private consultation. Below it sits the Beyer Clock and Watch Museum for the horology-minded.

A jewel-box basement museum beneath the Beyer store on Bahnhofstrasse, tracing timekeeping from around 1400 BC to the present across some 270 objects — sundials, tower clocks, pocket watches and the prototype of the first quartz wristwatch. A short, rich stop that gives context before any watch purchase; a natural pairing for collectors.

The house that has stood at Paradeplatz since 1859, celebrated for its featherlight Luxemburgerli macarons and truffles. The upstairs café is a Zurich institution for a mid-morning coffee and cake; the boutique makes elegant, packable gifts to carry home. Reliable vegetarian sweets and a favourite treat for children and grandparents alike.

The Lake Zurich Navigation Company runs daily scheduled cruises from the Bürkliplatz quay, from short 1.5-hour loops to longer runs past the villa-lined 'Gold Coast' to Rapperswil, aboard motor vessels and classic paddle steamers. Book a Dream Boat dinner or brunch cruise for a private-feeling occasion; the calm water and Alpine backdrop suit multi-generation groups.

The right-bank promenade runs from Bürkliplatz along the Utoquai to the parks at Zürichhorn — swans, plane trees, the Chinese Garden and, on clear days, the Alps mirrored in the water. A gentle, level walk perfect for grandparents and an evening stroll after dinner. Stop at the Pavillon Le Corbusier along the way.

venues.n: Summer swimming at the Badis (Seebad Enge & Utoquai)
venues.d: Zurich swims in its own lake and rivers in summer. Seebad Enge is a stylish lakeside lido with a sauna and a bar; the historic wooden Seebad Utoquai has welcomed swimmers off its docks for over 120 years. Clean, cold, and quintessentially local — a refreshing morning dip before the day's sightseeing.

Switzerland's largest art museum, expanded by a luminous David Chipperfield extension. The collection runs from Old Masters and a deep Giacometti holding to Munch, the Impressionists and Pipilotti Rist's immersive installations. Admission to the permanent collection is free on Wednesdays; a private docent can tailor a focused hour for the family.

Switzerland's only major museum of non-European art, set in three historic villas in the emerald Rieterpark above the lake. Strong Indian, Chinese, Japanese, African and Himalayan collections — of particular resonance for Indian visitors — shown with real care. Combine with a stroll through the park for one of the city's calmest cultural afternoons.

Three floors of football history opposite Bahnhof Enge, with the original World Cup trophy on display, over 1,000 pieces of memorabilia and hands-on digital stations. A genuine highlight for football-mad teenagers and a fine rainy-day option; interactive enough to hold a mixed-age group.

The 871-metre mountain rising over the city, reached in about 20 minutes on the S10 train from the main station. From the lookout tower the whole of Zurich, the lake and, on clear days, the Alps unfold below. Gentle ridge walks, a summit restaurant and easy access make it a relaxed half-day with sweeping photographs.

One of Europe's most respected zoos, home to over 300 species, the vast Kaeng Krachan elephant park and the Lewa Savanna. Its showpiece is the Masoala Rainforest hall — a walk-through slice of Madagascar with free-flying birds, lemurs and dense green heat. A sure hit for children; reach it by tram or the funicular up the Zürichberg.

The Lindt & Sprüngli chocolate experience just outside the city, built around the world's tallest chocolate fountain at over nine metres, an interactive museum and a generous free tasting zone. Book a chocolate-making workshop for the family, and stock the largest Lindt shop in the world with gifts to carry home. Reachable by a short train or lake boat.

A restored 19th-century railway viaduct whose brick arches now hold design boutiques, a covered market hall and cafés — the beating heart of the city's reinvented industrial west. Graze the market hall for lunch, browse Swiss makers, and feel a grittier, more creative Zurich than Bahnhofstrasse.

An urban garden of shipping-container shops, a summer beer garden and street food beneath the Prime Tower — at 126 metres one of Switzerland's tallest buildings. A relaxed, in-the-know spot for a sundowner; ride up to the Clouds restaurant and bar in the tower for a skyline view over the district.

A grand 19th-century opera house on the lakefront, one of Europe's most respected houses for opera and ballet. Book a box for an evening in your finest; the neo-Baroque interior and the square outside make it an occasion in itself. A concierge can secure premium seats and pre-theatre dining nearby.

The 1895 concert hall of the Tonhalle Orchester Zürich, its acoustics ranked among the finest in Europe and its gilded interior beautifully restored. An evening of world-class symphonic music in an intimate, ornate room — a refined alternative to a night at the opera.

A small, romantic city-centre garden laid out on a former bastion, with a historic domed palm house and quiet terraced lawns. A green pause a few minutes from the shopping — pleasant for grandparents and children needing a breather between museums.

The last building Le Corbusier designed — his only work in steel and glass — a jewel of primary-coloured panels set in the lakeside park at Zürichhorn. Open roughly May to November; a short, distinctive stop for design lovers, easily folded into a lake promenade walk.

The tiny room at Spiegelgasse 1 where the Dada movement was born in 1916, now a café-bar and cultural space. A niche but genuine piece of art history tucked into the Old Town lanes — worth a coffee and a glance for the culturally curious.

In the leafy Fluntern cemetery on the Zürichberg lies James Joyce, who spent his final years in Zurich, marked by a seated bronze statue of the writer, book in hand. A quiet literary pilgrimage that pairs naturally with a visit to the nearby zoo.

A perfectly preserved medieval town on the Rhine, its main square ringed by half-timbered houses covered in vivid painted frescoes and oriel windows. Small, walkable and postcard-pretty — an easy, gentle addition to a Rhine Falls day, well suited to a relaxed pace with grandparents.

Year-round glacier and snow at 3,000-plus metres, reached from the monastery village of Engelberg via the world's first rotating cable car, plus a cliff walk suspension bridge and a glacier cave. The most reliable place near Zurich to put the family in real Alpine snow whatever the season.

The wooded ridge above the city, laced with easy trails, clearings and a wildlife park, reached by tram or funicular. A green, restorative morning away from the crowds, with occasional views down to the lake — pleasant for a slow family walk before a zoo or cemetery visit nearby.

A stack of 17 rusted shipping containers forming the flagship of Zurich's cult Freitag brand, whose bags are cut from used truck tarpaulins — climb to the top for a view over the western district. A quirky design pilgrimage and a distinctly Swiss, one-of-a-kind gift to take home.

A serene walled Chinese garden by the lake, a gift from Zurich's twin city Kunming, with pavilions, a koi pond and ornate gates. A small, tranquil detour on the lakeside promenade — a quiet, contemplative pause that reads well with grandparents.
Cocktails mixed beneath real Miró, Klee and Chagall, under lamps Diego Giacometti made for the room — a Zurich rite since the 1960s.
Over a thousand spirits and a legendary whisky wall, with live jazz some nights — one of Europe's most respected hotel bars.
A spirits pilgrimage — 1,600-odd bottles, rare whiskies and forgotten liqueurs, mixed with quiet precision.
Zurich's highest bar — the 35th floor, the Limmat valley and the Alps through the glass, best caught at sunset.
A round bar in the old Urania observatory tower — the Old Town, the lake and the Alps wrapped around you.
